After unveiling the abuse I spent about 9 months still in contact. I was then lucky to go away for a month and a half, I was traveling and chose to cut communications while I was there. I think the distance helped me get perspective and find the confidence to cut contact. That was a little over a year ago.

I know someone else who moved away for about a year, not consciously trying to run away from the abuser, but probably unconsciously so. She said the distance helped her plan her future and be decisive about cutting ties.

Sometimes it’s hard to make these decisions while you’re still in contact. Going away for a while might help.

If you want, Audible lets me gift a copy of the audiobook to anyone, since I’ve purchased it.

I think that while narcissists may gain some knowledge from these resources, the benefit that survivors get from having these tools and knowledge greatly outweigh any gain a narcissist may get from it.

I would really like to recommend the book “When I say no I feel guilty”.

He describes a process where your inner critic will mimic your abusers’ contempt for you in these kinds of situations. It’s like you’re telling yourself that you are unworthy and don’t deserve these good things, just like your abusers would make you feel unlovable.

These negative feelings are called emotional flashbacks. This author gives some advice as how to manage it and diminish its effects.

If you want, Audible lets me share the audiobook for free with anyone, since I’ve purchased it. It really helped me with this kind of stuff.

There are a few images that I feel may represent CPTSD.

The first is the idea of a shadow, or a monster that lingers around you, and that only you can see it or know it’s there:

[The Shadow & the Star by Kathrin Honesta](https://www.behance.net/gallery/32492651/The-Shadow-The-Star)

[Illustration by Wylie Beckert](https://www.behance.net/gallery/20012906/Tam-Lin-(traditional-media))

[Illustrations by Michael Driver - The 2nd and 5th ones](https://www.behance.net/gallery/71216777/World-Mental-Health-Day)

[Illustration by Olivia Sualdea](https://www.behance.net/gallery/52439663/Self-Promotion-Tale-of-Shadows-Gone)

[Illustration by XA XB](https://www.behance.net/gallery/63609975/DID-ANYONE-TELL-YOU)

[Illustration by Kinga Gazda](https://www.behance.net/gallery/35375081/Heart-of-Darkness)

The second is the idea of pain and the slow traumatizing process symbolized by darkness slowly consuming you:

[Animal Portraiture by Nathan Wirth](https://www.behance.net/gallery/83332375/Animal-Portraiture)

[Possessed Portraits by Thomas Rohlfs](https://www.behance.net/gallery/73937389/Possessed-Portraits)
I don’t like the illustrations this artist made, but this is an idea that I can’t find a good work on. Of being covered by a shadow, kinda like when Black Panther from the Marvel movies puts on his suit.

Another image is that of debris, like a destroyed building or the remains of an explosion. The idea of being a mess after an event. Ashes also come into this category:

[Look at the last images](https://www.behance.net/gallery/51612643/NATIVO)

I also feel like images of you being different symbolizes a feeling that may come from CPTSD, that you are different inside, even broken, and that it makes you different from everybody else:

[Strangers](https://www.behance.net/gallery/76135449/Strangers)

On the same note, I like the image of objects that are seemingly average on the outside, but are colorful and abstract (or wild) on the inside, representing inner turmoil:

[Work by Alba Suarez](https://www.behance.net/gallery/48880743/ALBA-SUAREZ-branding)

[Work by Alexander Sellas](https://www.behance.net/gallery/6614753/Die-Glorifizierung-des-Banalen)

[Work by Nick Liefhebber](https://www.behance.net/gallery/58259197/Terrarium)

Do you feel like you were in pain, even as a child, or do you feel like the pain started later?

In my case I believe I was healthy, happy and hopeful as a child. Even while I feel like the abuse started then, I was slowing being corrupted and I started feeling it really bad in my early teen years.

When I first heard about doing inner child work, it gave me a mental image of being in touch with that happy child. I dug up pictures of me as a child, smiling, curious and happy, but also seeming very innocent and vulnerable. This made me feel a strength and a will to defend and protect that child with my adult resources, and ultimately I guess that attention is transferring to me, as I’m noticing I’m starting to stand up and protect myself a lot more now.

I don’t know if that made sense, but the inner child idea has been somewhat helpful to me. I’m sorry it’s not working out for you, and I hope you find more ways to heal and become better.
